title: Material properties of wooden surfaces used in interiors and sensory stimulation
review_question: To determine (i) the material properties of wood which are associated with sensory stimulation, and (ii) to specify relevant recommendations or requirements which should be fulfilled when covering interiors with wooden surfaces.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies analyzing the correlation between sensory stimulation from wooden surfaces in interiors and related changes in physiological responses. English-language studies published between 2000 and 2018. Subject areas: medicine, neuroscience, biochemistry, genetics and molecular biology, psychology, material science, social science, pharmacology, toxicology and pharmaceutics, immunology and microbiology, and nursing. Excluded studies not meeting these criteria.

findings.antecedent: Number of knots exposed in interior wooden surfaces
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: A study by Nakamura and Kondo (2007) shows a positive linear relationship between the number of knots exposed in wooden surfaces in interiors and eye fatigue

findings.antecedent: Wood color (long-wave, yellow-to-red hue)
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: long-wave colours with a yellow-to-red hue can improve cog-nitive performance.

findings.antecedent: Aromatic lignin component in wood
findings.consequent: Eye comfort and health (absorption of ultraviolet light, prevention of retina degradation)
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: the aromatic lignin com-ponent in wood can absorb a high amount of ultraviolet light (Kutz 2005), creating a comfortable environment for the eye.

findings.antecedent: Anatomical level relief structure of wood surfaces
findings.consequent: Surface glare, luminance value, eye fatigue, eye strain, headaches, perceived stress
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: the anatomical level relief structure of wood surfaces induces light to scatter and diminish surface glare... reduced glare and an adequate luminance value can decrease the incidence of eye fatigue, eye strain and headaches... thereby reducing perceived stress

findings.antecedent: Wood surface treatments (stain, clear varnish, film-forming paint)
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: wood surface treatments can provide uniform light distribution and thereby decrease per-ceived glare

findings.antecedent: Visual stimulation from interior wooden surfaces
findings.consequent: Physiological responses (blood pressure, heart rate, rCBF), perceived stress
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: Generally, visual stimulation associated with wooden surfaces in interiors was found to have positive effects on physiological responses, which resulted in a reduction in respondents' perceived stress.

findings.antecedent: Higher moisture content in wood
findings.source: Material properties associated with auditory stimulation
findings.quote: A higher moisture content can deterio-rate the acoustic properties of wood, since it changes the microstructure of the cell walls

findings.antecedent: Surface treatments (wood stain, clear varnish, film-forming paint)
findings.source: Material properties associated with auditory stimulation
findings.quote: Surface treatments including wood stain, clear varnish, and film-forming paint, can affect acoustic performance by modi-fying damping, stiffness, and mass

findings.antecedent: Wood density
findings.source: Material properties associated with auditory stimulation
findings.quote: Density is the other impor-tant factor which characterises the acoustic performance of wood

findings.antecedent: Auditory stimulation from wooden buildings (heavy floor-impact sounds, various sounds)
findings.consequent: Physiological responses (blood pressure, peripheral blood flow, heart rate, skin conductance, respiratory rate), individual sensitivity
findings.source: Material properties associated with auditory stimulation
findings.quote: physiological responses to sound are indeed dependent on individual sensitivity more than on the sounds or their pressure levels.

findings.antecedent: Chemical composition of wood (volatile extractives, monoterpenes)
findings.source: Material properties associated with olfactory stimulation
findings.quote: The effects of olfactory stimulation from wood on physiologi-cal responses depend strongly on the chemical composition of the wood, including volatile extractives

findings.antecedent: Moisture content of wood
findings.source: Material properties associated with olfactory stimulation
findings.quote: The emission of extractives is mainly affected by moisture content

findings.antecedent: Monoterpenes group of substances (composition and amount)
findings.consequent: Olfactory stimulation, physiological responses (oxy-Hb, HRV, heart rate, CNV, natural killer cells, stress hormones)
findings.source: Material properties associated with olfactory stimulation
findings.quote: The composition and amount of monoter-penes in wood is strongly dependent upon a tree's age, its species, its genetics and the time of the year

findings.antecedent: Plywood (emitting Formaldehyde)
findings.source: Material properties associated with olfactory stimulation
findings.quote: The results show a signifi-cant change in oxy-Hb when respondents were exposed to plywood. This was because plywood emitted a higher quan-tity of Formaldehyde than the other samples.

findings.antecedent: Individual sensitivity (gender)
findings.source: Material properties associated with olfactory stimulation
findings.quote: The results presented showed a tendency for women to be more sensitive towards olfactory stimulation than men.

findings.antecedent: Thermal conductivity of wood and wood-based materials
findings.consequent: Heat flux, skin temperature, perceived warmth/pleasantness
findings.source: Material properties associated with tactile stimulation
findings.quote: the thermal conductivity of wood and wood-based materials is lower than other materials commonly used to cover interiors... perceived as having a warm and pleasant material.

findings.antecedent: Moisture content or density of wood
findings.source: Material properties associated with tactile stimulation
findings.quote: The thermal conductivity of wood is increased by augmenting either moisture content or density

findings.antecedent: Grain direction (longitudinal vs. radial/tangential)
findings.source: Material properties associated with tactile stimulation
findings.quote: the thermal conductivity of wood in the longitudinal direction can be 1.5-2.8 times greater than in the radial or tangential directions

findings.antecedent: Heat treatments, chemical treatments, surface treatments (modifying/preserving moisture content)
findings.source: Material properties associated with tactile stimulation
findings.quote: The thermal conductivity of wood can be altered by apply-ing heat treatments, chemical treatments and surface treat-ments

findings.antecedent: Tactile stimulation from wooden surfaces
findings.consequent: Physiological responses (systolic blood pressure, skin temperature), perceived stress
findings.source: Material properties associated with tactile stimulation
findings.quote: touching wooden surfaces has mainly positive effects on physiological responses, and can reduce perceived stress.

findings.antecedent: Reflectance value of walls, ceilings, and floors in office buildings
findings.source: Material properties associated with visual stimulation
findings.quote: The Room and Light standard demands a reflectance value of 60%, 80% and 20% for walls, ceilings, and floors in office buildings respectively

findings.antecedent: Moisture content for wooden floors
findings.source: Material properties associated with auditory stimulation
findings.quote: the moisture content for wooden floors should be between 7% to 9%.

findings.antecedent: Wood treatments containing Creosote, Arsenic or Pentachlorophenol chemicals
findings.source: Material properties associated with olfactory stimulation
findings.quote: Living Building Challenge standard prohibit any use of wood treatments which contain Creosote, Arsenic or Pentachlorophenol chemicals.

synthesis_conclusions: Visual stimulation from wooden surfaces depends on knots, color, structure, and surface treatment, but no specific recommendations or requirements were found in standards or certifications.

Physiological responses to auditory stimulation are strongly dependent on individual sensitivity rather than sound impact sources or pressure levels. Material properties like wood composition, surface treatment, mounting, and geometry affect acoustic performance, but no specific recommendations were found.

Olfactory stimulation is strongly dependent on the chemical composition of wood, including volatile extractives. Previous studies showed inconsistencies and lacked material property explanations. Only the Living Building Challenge prohibits certain chemical treatments.

Tactile stimulation depends on the heat flux and thermal conductivity of materials. Wood has lower thermal conductivity and is perceived as warm and pleasant, but no specific recommendations for its use based on this property were found.
Overall, there is a lack of knowledge regarding the specific material properties of wood and the degree to which they affect sensory stimulation and subsequent physiological/psychological responses.
evidence_gaps: Lack of knowledge regarding specific material properties of wood and their degree of effect on sensory stimulation.
Previous studies had small sample sizes, limited age ranges, and short exposure times.
Lack of insight into how changing experiment settings could affect results.
Lack of described correlations between respondents' sensitivity and sensory stimulation.
Need for future studies to evaluate and describe material specifications.
Future studies should consider other indoor environmental quality factors (artificial lighting, air quality, sounds).
More studies needed in different environments (residential, educational, commercial, hospitals).
Need for longitudinal studies to provide information on long-term effects.
heterogeneity_sources: Lack of material specifications in primary studies
Inconsistency in results across studies (e.g., olfactory stimulation from different wood species)
Lack of control for experiment settings
Lack of correlation between individual sensitivity and sensory stimulation

moderators.effect: Influences physiological responses to auditory and olfactory stimulation (e.g., women more sensitive to olfactory stimulation than men).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Physiological responses to sound are dependent on individual sensitivity more than on sound impact sources or pressure levels. Women tend to be more sensitive towards olfactory stimulation than men.

limitations: Results are mainly limited due to the small sample size, the small age range and the short exposure time of the primary studies.

Majority of the studies provided neither insight into how changing experiment settings could affect the results, nor described the correlations between the respondents' sensitivity toward sensory stimulation.
Earlier studies provided no explanation regarding the material properties of wood which are associated with sensory stimulation.
